strengths: Comprehensive experimental validation across controlled settings (simulated noise on 6 image datasets) and realistic large-scale web data (DataComp 10M/100M samples), demonstrating broad applicability
Strong empirical correlations with dataset quality: F1-scores >90% for mislabeled sample detection and Pearson correlation 0.958 between mimic scores and performance gains in DataComp experiments
Practical framework that avoids dependencies on downstream evaluation datasets or expensive specialized model training by leveraging publicly available pretrained models
Clear presentation of core idea: gradient alignment with reference direction is intuitive and well-motivated through compelling problem framing in introduction
Useful contributions to automated data selection that could reduce computational costs for model training and improve sample efficiency
weaknesses: Weak theoretical justification: paper lacks principled analysis of WHY gradient alignment with reference model indicates sample value beyond intuition; reference model dependency unexplored (no sensitivity analysis for reference quality degradation, marginal improvements, or temporal dynamics as ℓ(θ_ref)−ℓ(θ_t) changes)

Significant experimental concerns: acknowledged broken DataComp URLs compromise reproducibility and leaderboard comparability; weak Pearson correlation (0.279) between mimic score and CLIP score on medium-scale data contradicts narrative; no statistical significance testing, error bars, or confidence intervals reported

Methodological issues: Equation 1 normalization not unit-normalized (divides by ‖v_t‖_2 not normalized), creating unexplained temporal dependence on model-reference distance; softmax normalization choice appears arbitrary with only temperature ablated; temperature selection rules for new domains not justified

Limited scope: simulation experiments only on image classification; no language model experiments despite LLM mentions in introduction; limited architecture diversity (primarily ViT and CLIP); no computational cost analysis for per-sample gradient computation

Stage 2 design concerns: weak supervision aggregation via Snorkel seems orthogonal to core contribution with no comparison to simpler alternatives (majority voting, averaging); F1-based evaluation on simulated data but no Stage 2 filtering comparison against baseline methods (GraNd/AGRA/Grad-Match)

Missing critical analysis: no explanation for why image encoder outperforms text encoder (Table 3); no failure case analysis; Figure 5 caption analysis potentially confounded (short/long captions may reflect processing difficulty not quality); reference model training cost not discussed
Modest improvements in realistic settings: DataComp small scale 0.131→0.145 (10.7%), medium scale 0.254→0.268 (5.5%), real but not exceptional given added complexity

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Data quality for large-scale foundation models is important and limitations of existing approaches are clearly articulated
Simple and intuitive formulation: The core Mimic Score metric (gradient projection) is mathematically straightforward and implementable
Comprehensive experimental scope: Evaluation across 6 image datasets with simulated noise and 10M/100M scale DataComp data with 38 downstream tasks
Consistent empirical improvements: Shows gains across datasets; Pearson correlation of 0.958 between mimic scores and performance gains (Figure 4b)
Practical approach: Uses publicly available pretrained models as reference, eliminating need for custom reference model training in some scenarios
weaknesses: Lack of theoretical justification: No formal analysis of why gradient projection onto reference weight direction should indicate data quality; entire approach rests on intuition without theoretical grounding

Circular reasoning in DataComp experiments: Reference model trained on 1.4B samples; curating smaller 10M/100M datasets to 'mimic' this reference essentially recovers pre-curated samples rather than discovering principles; Table 5 shows only 42.6% overlap with DataComp'23 best dataset

Confounded reference model quality: Sensitivity to reference model quality is not systematically studied; simulation requires unrealistic clean reference training; main experiments conflate method effectiveness with access to extremely powerful reference model

Limited insight into mechanism: Figure 5 shows method primarily filters by caption length (too short/long)—a trivial heuristic requiring no gradients; Figure 6 shows only 0.279 correlation with CLIP scores, indicating limited capture of deep semantic quality

Weak baseline comparisons: GraNd, AGRA, Grad-Match perform poorly in simulation (Table 1) suggesting implementation issues; no comparison to recent selection methods; CLIP Score baseline uses different model (unfair comparison); no comparison to simpler alternatives like reference model confidence scoring

Stage 2 disconnected from core contribution: Uses existing Snorkel framework for aggregation; feels orthogonal to Mimic Score innovation; no ablation on aggregation method; adds complexity without clear justification
Computational cost unaddressed: Per-sample gradient computation for 100M samples is expensive; no runtime analysis or comparison; scalability to larger datasets unclear

Overstated claims: Claims of bypassing downstream dataset needs misleading (requires powerful reference model); 'automating' data selection overstated (requires threshold/temperature selection); 'fine-grained insights' not supported
Limited novelty: Gradient-based selection well-established (GraNd, AGRA, Grad-Match); adding reference model direction is incremental; weak supervision (Snorkel) is existing work
Incomplete ablations: No systematic ablation on reference model quality; limited exploration of which layers to mimic; no ablation on Stage 2 method; missing comparison to influence functions
Reproducibility concerns: DataComp has broken URLs (acknowledged), exact reproduction impossible; no code availability; 100M-scale experiments prohibitively expensive to reproduce
Hyperparameter selection not principled: Temperature τ selection lacks justification; Table 6 shows sensitivity but no method for setting τ on new datasets

strengths: Novel and intuitive core idea: Using reference model weight direction as a guide for sample quality assessment is creative and well-motivated

Comprehensive experimental validation: Controlled label-noise experiments on 6 datasets with precise mislabel detection (F1 > 0.90), plus large-scale DataComp experiments (10M-100M samples) with consistent improvements
Strong empirical results: Outperforms gradient-based baselines (GraNd, AGRA, Grad-Match); mimic scores show strong correlation with dataset quality (r=0.958) and performance gains
Practical two-stage framework: Stage 1 enables real-time training improvement via gradient reweighting; Stage 2 automates filter design post-training using weak supervision
Clear presentation: Well-written with effective figures; Algorithm 1 and experimental details support reproducibility; good interpretability (e.g., caption-length alignment in Figure 5)
Multiple demonstrated applications: Noise detection, dataset quality assessment, filtering complementarity with CLIP Score, predicting pretraining dataset membership
weaknesses: Lack of theoretical justification: No formal analysis of why gradient-direction alignment with reference model should correlate with data quality; missing connection to optimization theory, influence functions, or generalization bounds; purely empirical validation

Critical dependence on reference model quality severely limits applicability: DataComp experiments use a model trained on 1.4B samples (far beyond typical practitioner access); limited sensitivity analysis to reference model degradation; Appendix A.1 dismisses this risk with vague suggestions

Significant experimental caveats undermine large-scale claims: Footnote 1 discloses broken URLs in DataComp making results potentially incomparable to leaderboard; this deserves prominent discussion not relegation to footnote; limited Stage 2 baselines (only CLIP Score, basic filtering)

Incomplete technical analysis: (1) Temperature τ is critical hyperparameter requiring tuning with limited guidance; (2) No ablation on layer choice despite claiming only last MLP layer works best; (3) No computational cost analysis for expensive per-sample gradients on 100M samples; (4) Role of Snorkel vs. mimic scores unclear

Limited scope and generalization: Evaluated only on vision tasks (image classification, CLIP); despite motivating with NLP foundation models (LLaMA-3.1), no NLP experiments; generalization to other modalities/tasks/architectures unknown

Insufficient mechanistic understanding: Figure 5 suggests rediscovery of handcrafted heuristics (caption length); no failure case analysis; 42.6% DataComp overlap finding underdeveloped; missing ablations on weak supervision aggregation strategy
Moderate correlation with existing methods: CLIP Score correlation only r=0.279 on random samples (Figure 6) raises questions about independence and complementarity
Statistical rigor issues: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; single runs reported without variance assessment; some DataComp improvements modest (0.254→0.258)

strengths: Clear motivation and well-executed approach to an important problem (data curation for large-scale models)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple scales, from controlled noise simulation to 100M-sample DataComp experiments
Practical efficiency benefits: avoids validation-set dependencies, leverages public models, demonstrates 20.7% training step reduction and lower memory/runtime than alternatives
Strong dataset quality assessment results (0.958 Pearson correlation between mimic scores and performance gains)
Two-stage framework design is thoughtful, with online re-weighting improving convergence and offline aggregation providing reusable filters
Extensive ablations and robustness analysis (Appendix F), showing method remains competitive even with degraded reference models
weaknesses: Theoretical analysis is weak: Theorem A.4's learning rate conditions are complex and rarely verifiable; core assumption (θ_ref resides in 'more optimal weight space') lacks rigorous justification—reference models are merely trained differently, not guaranteed to approach the same optimum
Empirical improvements are modest (1-3% typical gains over baselines, ~1.2% relative on DataComp) with no error bars or statistical significance testing
Core technical contribution is limited: mimic score is a straightforward projection (⟨−g_{i,t}, v_t⟩/∥v_t∥); gradient-based sample scoring is well-established

Reproducibility concerns: broken DataComp URLs acknowledged but inadequately addressed; no code availability; simulated reference models (trained on clean data) are artificial compared to real external models
Predicting pretraining dataset experiment (Table 5, 42.6% overlap) reveals method sensitivity to reference model training data, raising concerns about bias amplification—inadequately discussed

Snorkel-based weak supervision aggregation is ad-hoc; alternatives not explored; introduces additional hyperparameters (binarization method, clustering threshold) without principled selection guidelines
Limited practical guidance on reference model selection in deployment; unclear how to handle multiple candidate models or biased reference models

Scope limitations: primarily vision/multimodal; minimal language model evaluation; moderate correlation (0.279) in Figure 5 between mimic and CLIP scores on random samples raises questions about what method captures

strengths: Well-written paper with clear motivation and systematic presentation
Comprehensive experiments spanning simulation (6 datasets), small-scale (10M), and medium-scale (100M) settings
Efficiency analysis demonstrating computational advantages over Rho-Loss and approximated influence functions (Appendix E)
Dual-stage framework providing both online reweighting and offline filtering flexibility
Thorough ablation studies on temperature selection, layer choice, and reference model degradation quality
weaknesses: Limited novelty: combines straightforward application of reference model guidance with standard gradient alignment measurement; Theorem A.4 uses conventional proof techniques
Inconsistent empirical results: method underperforms on STL10 (Table 1) and shows high variance across datasets; average improvements of only 1-3% on large-scale tasks

Theory-practice gap: assumes θ_ref closer to optimum than θ_t early in training; uses public CLIP models trained on different data; convergence condition in Theorem A.4 is complex and impractical to verify
Fundamental reference model dependency inadequately addressed: no systematic guidance for practitioners on reference model selection; Table 11 shows significant degradation with weaker references
Weak correlation between proposed metric and quality: Figure 5 shows correlation of only 0.279 between mimic score and CLIP score; critical issue buried in text
Table 4 reveals CLIP Score (0.321) substantially outperforms Grad-Mimic alone (0.258); method's value is primarily as secondary filter, not standalone approach
Stage 2 design issues: binarization schemes are ad-hoc and lossy; using Snorkel LabelModel appears overengineered without ablation on aggregation methods
Reproducibility concerns: broken DataComp URLs, heavy reliance on appendix (22 pages total), no mentioned code release, temperature hyperparameter requires dataset-specific tuning
Limited comparison to recent baselines: GraNd/AGRA/Grad-Match are from 2021; approximated influence function comparison confined to Appendix D
Claims overstate results: abstract emphasizes '20.7% fewer steps' (Figure 4) and '4.7M fewer samples' but these represent marginal gains (4.7% of 100M) in narrow settings

strengths: Clear, intuitive method with simple mimic score computation that effectively aligns training samples with reference model weights

Comprehensive experimental validation: controlled experiments on 6 datasets, large-scale DataComp experiments, multiple baseline comparisons (GraNd, AGRA, Grad-Match, Rho-Loss, influence functions), and extensive ablations
Strong empirical results: 20.7% reduction in training steps on DataComp, removes 4.7M samples while maintaining performance, strong correlation (0.958) between mimic scores and performance gains
Practical efficiency advantages: no need for noise-free validation sets, computational overhead comparable to GraNd, complementary to existing filtering methods

Thorough presentation: clear figures (especially Figure 1 showing visual quality alignment), detailed algorithms and configurations in appendices, honest treatment of limitations and robustness under degraded reference models
Theoretical analysis (Theorem A.4) characterizing convergence conditions where method outperforms standard gradient descent
weaknesses: Incremental novelty: core contribution combines existing ideas (gradient-based reweighting from GraNd/AGRA/Grad-Match with reference models from Rho-Loss); weak supervision aggregation uses off-the-shelf Snorkel

Theory-practice gap: Theorem A.4 provides restrictive sufficient conditions (small η, small κ, small ε) that are difficult to control in practice; theory assumes convex losses while practice is non-convex; improvement bound is relative to vanilla GD, not stronger baselines

Critical DataComp reproducibility issue: authors acknowledge broken URLs in DataComp dataset, making results not directly comparable to leaderboard and undermining one of main large-scale validation experiments

Reference model dependency inadequately addressed: core assumption that θ_ref resides in 'more optimal weight space' lacks formal justification; no guidance on verifying reference model suitability for new domains; Table 11 shows noticeable performance drops with degraded reference models

Methodological concerns: reference models in simulation trained on clean data with different seeds (artificial scenario); limited ablation on whether binarization+aggregation complexity is necessary; comparison to other data selection paradigms (embedding similarity, uncertainty) is limited

Predicting pretraining dataset result (Table 5): 42.6% overlap with reference model training data suggests method may bias toward reproducing reference model's data rather than finding universally good samples; raises concerns about unintended applications
Statistical rigor: no confidence intervals or standard deviations reported; most results appear to be single runs; differences in Tables 1-2 are sometimes small and need significance testing

Incomplete design justifications: why Snorkel specifically for aggregation; temperature parameter τ requires tuning with limited guidance; gradient computation overhead not isolated in timing comparisons
